title: On-air terms & phrases
intro: Understand the words you hear during amateur radio conversations. Search a term, read its meaning, and see a short example of how it is used.
guidance: Plain language works well on voice. Q codes began as compact signals for telegraphy; some are common in speech, while speed requests such as QRS mainly belong to Morse operation.
Listen before speaking and leave pauses for other stations. The call signs in square brackets are placeholders for the actual station identities.
A question mark changes a written or Morse Q signal into a question. In spoken conversation, use a clear question or statement rather than relying on punctuation you cannot hear.

entries.meaning: A general call inviting another amateur station to answer.
entries.example: CQ CQ, this is [your call sign], calling CQ and listening.
entries.note: Listen and check that a frequency is available before calling. On a local repeater, announcing your call sign and monitoring is usually more appropriate.

entries.meaning: A general call asking for distant stations, often outside the caller’s own region or country.
entries.example: CQ DX, this is [your call sign].
entries.note: What counts as DX depends on the band and the caller’s stated target. Listen to any geographic restrictions.

entries.meaning: A call seeking short contacts in a radio contest.
entries.example: CQ contest, this is [your call sign].
entries.note: Listen for the required exchange and read that contest’s rules before joining.

entries.meaning: The station identifier assigned for amateur operation. Use it to identify yourself and the station you are calling.
entries.example: [Other call sign], this is [your call sign].
entries.note: Give your actual assigned call sign. Names and nicknames do not replace station identification.

entries.meaning: Introduces the identity of the station speaking.
entries.example: [Other call sign], this is [your call sign].
entries.note: Putting the called station first and your own identity second makes the direction of a call clear.

entries.meaning: Listening on a frequency and available to answer a call.
entries.example: [Your call sign] monitoring.
entries.note: Common on repeaters. It announces your presence without a long CQ call.

entries.meaning: A radio contact or conversation between stations.
entries.example: Thanks for the QSO.
entries.note: In casual speech, having a QSO means making a contact; the formal Q signal concerns communication with another station.

entries.meaning: A distant station or a long-distance contact.
entries.example: I heard some DX on the band this morning.
entries.note: Distance is relative to the band and conditions; DX does not always mean another country.

entries.meaning: A relaxed, extended conversation over amateur radio.
entries.example: Would you like a short ragchew?
entries.note: Keep listening for other callers and leave gaps so the frequency can be shared.

entries.meaning: An experienced amateur who helps someone learn the hobby.
entries.example: My Elmer helped me set up the antenna.
entries.note: It is a friendly mentoring term, not a certificate or official position.

entries.meaning: The specific information passed during a contact, especially in a contest.
entries.example: Please repeat the serial number in your exchange.
entries.note: An exchange may include a signal report, number or location; each event defines its own required information.

entries.meaning: Many stations trying to contact the same station at once.
entries.example: There is a pileup calling that DX station.
entries.note: Listen to whom the station is answering and whether it has announced split operation. Avoid calling over an existing reply.

entries.meaning: Asks whether the frequency is in use.
entries.example: On voice: Is this frequency in use? This is [your call sign].
entries.note: A question mark makes the written or Morse Q signal a question. Plain language is clear on voice.
entries.question: Are you busy / is this frequency in use?
entries.statement: QRL: I am busy / the frequency is in use.

entries.meaning: Asks which station is calling you.
entries.example: QRZ? Please give your call sign again.
entries.note: It is not a general test for an empty frequency; use Is this frequency in use? or QRL? for that.
entries.question: Who is calling me?
entries.statement: QRZ: You are being called by the named station.

entries.meaning: Change to another frequency.
entries.example: Let’s QSY to an agreed clear frequency.
entries.note: Check that the new frequency is available and suitable before transmitting.
entries.question: Shall I change frequency?
entries.statement: Change frequency / I am changing frequency.

entries.meaning: Your station’s location.
entries.example: My QTH is Mississauga, Ontario.
entries.note: A town or general location is normally enough for a casual conversation; you need not give a private street address.
entries.question: What is your location?
entries.statement: My location is the place stated.

entries.meaning: Acknowledges reception; also refers to confirming a radio contact.
entries.example: QSL, I copied your report.
entries.note: A QSL card or electronic QSL is a contact confirmation, which is a different use from an immediate on-air acknowledgement.
entries.question: Can you acknowledge receipt?

entries.meaning: Interference from another radio transmission.
entries.example: I have QRM from a nearby signal.
entries.note: Distinguish interfering signals from atmospheric noise (QRN) and fading (QSB).
entries.question: Are other signals interfering?

entries.meaning: Atmospheric static or noise, commonly associated with lightning.
entries.example: There is heavy QRN tonight.
entries.note: Local electrical noise can also mask a station; describe it directly if you are unsure of the source.
entries.question: Are you troubled by atmospheric noise?
entries.statement: I am troubled by atmospheric noise.

entries.meaning: Received signal strength is fading or changing with time.
entries.example: Your signal has QSB; please repeat the last sentence.
entries.note: A fading signal may be strong for one moment and difficult to copy a few seconds later.
entries.question: Is my signal fading?

entries.meaning: Reduce power; also the name commonly used for low-power operating.
entries.example: I am running QRP today.
entries.note: Specific low-power limits depend on the activity or contest. The term does not create a separate operating privilege.
entries.question: Shall I reduce power?

entries.meaning: Increase power; also shorthand for higher-power operation.
entries.example: I can increase power if that would help readability.
entries.note: Use only the power appropriate to the contact and your authorization.
entries.question: Shall I increase power?

entries.meaning: Stop transmitting; often used when closing down an operating session.
entries.example: I am going QRT now. Thanks for the contact.
entries.note: It describes ending transmissions, not a change to another frequency.
entries.question: Shall I stop transmitting?

entries.meaning: Wait; in formal use it relates to when a station will call again.
entries.example: QRX one minute, please.
entries.note: You may hear it used casually to mean stand by. On voice, specifying the waiting time in plain language is helpful.
entries.question: When will you call me again?
entries.statement: I will call again at the stated time; commonly used as wait.

entries.meaning: Ready to communicate or receive the next transmission.
entries.example: I am QRV for the net.
entries.note: Ready is a clear voice alternative.
entries.question: Are you ready?

entries.meaning: Send Morse code faster.
entries.example: QRQ slightly, please.
entries.note: This is a Morse-speed request. For voice, say that you can copy a faster speaking pace if needed.
entries.question: Shall I send faster?

entries.meaning: Send Morse code more slowly.
entries.example: QRS please.
entries.note: For spoken communication, Please speak more slowly is clearer than using a Morse-speed signal.
entries.question: Shall I send more slowly?

entries.meaning: Listening on another stated frequency.
entries.example: The DX station says QSX five kilohertz up.
entries.note: Listen for the exact receive frequency or range. In split operation, the called station’s listening frequency is where callers transmit.
entries.question: Will you listen on the stated frequency?
entries.statement: I am listening on the stated frequency.

entries.meaning: A description of how well another station is being received.
entries.example: You are readable, but your signal is fading.
entries.note: Describe what you actually hear. A meter reading alone does not explain readability.

entries.meaning: A voice signal report giving readability (1–5) and signal strength (1–9).
entries.example: Your report is five and seven.
entries.note: The first number tells how easy the speech is to understand. The second describes received signal strength.

entries.meaning: Readability, signal strength and tone: a three-part report used especially for Morse code.
entries.example: Your Morse signal is five nine nine.
entries.note: Readability uses 1–5, strength 1–9, and tone 1–9. Voice normally omits the tone digit and uses RS.

entries.meaning: An RS report: readability 5 and signal strength 9.
entries.example: You are five nine here.
entries.note: It does not mean 59 percent. Do not automatically give 59 if you cannot actually read the station.

entries.meaning: An RST report: readability 5, strength 9, tone 9.
entries.example: Thanks, your RST is five nine nine.
entries.note: The third digit describes Morse tone quality. Voice normally uses two digits. In Morse contest reports, N may stand for 9, so 5NN means 599.

entries.meaning: An FM signal strong enough to suppress the background hiss in the receiver.
entries.example: You are full quieting into the repeater.
entries.note: It describes received FM noise, not guaranteed maximum readability or a universal S-meter value.

entries.meaning: Two stations transmitting at the same time on a shared channel.
entries.example: We doubled; please go ahead first.
entries.note: Pause and let one station speak. FM receivers may favour one signal, so the overlap may not be obvious to everyone.

entries.meaning: A request for a report on how your transmission is being received.
entries.example: [Your call sign], could someone give me a radio check?
entries.note: Ask about the problem you are testing, such as intelligibility, audio level or repeater access.

entries.meaning: Your transmission or message was received.
entries.example: Roger, I copied the location.
entries.note: It acknowledges reception; it does not by itself mean yes or I agree.

entries.meaning: Receive and understand what another station has said or sent.
entries.example: I copied the call sign, but missed your name.
entries.note: If only part was understood, say which part needs repeating.

entries.meaning: A request to repeat all or a specific part of a transmission.
entries.example: Say again the last three letters of your call sign.
entries.note: Naming the missing part saves time and avoids repeating information already understood.

entries.meaning: Introduces spelling with phonetic words so letters can be understood.
entries.example: My name is Kevin. I spell Kilo Echo Victor India November.
entries.note: Use standard phonetics when clarity matters, especially for call signs and names.

entries.meaning: Yes.
entries.example: Affirmative, I can hear you.
entries.note: It is an answer to a question, unlike Roger, which acknowledges reception.

entries.meaning: No, or a correction rejecting an incorrect detail.
entries.example: Negative, the last letter is Bravo.
entries.note: Add the correct detail when a mistake could cause confusion.

entries.meaning: I have finished this transmission and expect a reply.
entries.example: That is my report, over.
entries.note: Useful when turn-taking is unclear. Over and out expresses conflicting expectations; use the ending appropriate to your intention.

entries.meaning: The exchange is finished and no reply is expected.
entries.example: Message complete, out.
entries.note: Not needed at the end of every casual amateur transmission. Clear is also commonly heard when ending a contact.

entries.meaning: Wait briefly before continuing or answering.
entries.example: Stand by while I write that down.
entries.note: If practical, give an approximate wait time.

entries.meaning: An invitation for the other station to transmit.
entries.example: The station ending in Bravo, go ahead.
entries.note: Identify whom you are inviting if several stations are waiting.

entries.meaning: A request to enter an ongoing conversation, with local usage varying.
entries.example: [Your call sign], may I join you?
entries.note: On a repeater, give your call sign in a gap. Do not assume Break or Break break alone reliably communicates an emergency.

entries.meaning: Returns the speaking turn to another station.
entries.example: That is all from me. Back to you, [other call sign].
entries.note: In a group, name the next station so everyone knows whose turn it is.

entries.meaning: A standard word for each letter, used to spell call signs and other information clearly.
entries.example: I spell Alfa Bravo Charlie.
entries.note: Standard spellings include Alfa and Juliett. The reference table below lists all 26 words.

entries.meaning: An organized on-air gathering of stations.
entries.example: The local net starts this evening.
entries.note: A directed net uses a coordinator; a round-table conversation may use informal turn-taking.

entries.meaning: Net control station: the station coordinating a directed net.
entries.example: Net control, this is [your call sign] with a check-in.
entries.note: Follow the net control station’s check-in instructions and wait to be recognized.

entries.meaning: Registering your presence with a net.
entries.example: [Your call sign], Kevin, Mississauga, no traffic.
entries.note: Supply the information requested by that net. Some nets invite particular groups of stations in sequence.

entries.meaning: Messages or information a station needs to pass, often through an organized net.
entries.example: [Your call sign] with one item of traffic.
entries.note: No traffic means no message to pass; it does not mean the frequency is empty.

entries.meaning: An urgent communication involving an immediate threat to life or serious danger.
entries.example: Emergency traffic. [Your call sign]. I need assistance for an immediate danger at [location].
entries.note: State the emergency plainly, give the location and say what help is needed. Let genuine emergency communications take priority.

entries.meaning: Operating from a vehicle, often while travelling.
entries.example: [Your call sign] mobile.
entries.note: It describes the station’s situation; use your normal assigned identity and appropriate safe operating practices.

entries.meaning: Operating away from a usual fixed station, such as from a park or temporary site.
entries.example: [Your call sign] portable at the park.
entries.note: Portable describes the location or setup; it does not automatically mean low power.

entries.meaning: A direct amateur conversation in which stations normally share the same transmit and receive frequency.
entries.example: Shall we move to simplex?
entries.note: Agree on a suitable clear channel first. This is different from a typical repeater’s separate input and output frequencies.

entries.meaning: A station that receives and retransmits signals to extend coverage.
entries.example: You are reaching the repeater clearly.
entries.note: Listen first, leave pauses, and announce your call sign rather than keying it anonymously.

entries.meaning: A friendly closing meaning best regards.
entries.example: Thanks for the contact. Seventy-three, [your call sign].
entries.note: Common in both voice and Morse communication.

entries.meaning: An affectionate closing traditionally meaning love and kisses.
entries.example: You may hear a familiar operator finish with eighty-eight.
entries.note: It is more personal than 73 and is not a standard ending for every contact.

entries.meaning: Finished with a contact or releasing the channel.
entries.example: [Your call sign] clear, and listening.
entries.note: Clear and listening means you have ended that contact but remain available; clear and going off means you are leaving.

lines.text: [Your call sign], this is [other call sign]. Good afternoon.

lines.text: [Other call sign], this is [your call sign]. Thanks for coming back.

lines.text: I copied your call sign, but missed your name. Say again your name, please.

lines.speaker: Other station
lines.text: My name is Kevin. I spell Kilo Echo Victor India November.

lines.text: Thanks for the QSO. Seventy-three, [your call sign] clear and listening.
